\CRchapter{29}{The Word Stopped Twice}{Days 126–128 · Reed 7–9, Y.H. 813}{Low Kiln, the Weir and Sill}

\begin{CRchronicle}{29}
Reeds stood in the ruts at Reed’s opening, green at the broken ends and pale where frost had bitten the tips; the yard judged them by the carrying arm, never by a figure. Sella Vail carried the boy at the half-pace and gave the instruction to the wool and the river wind, never to the basket. A woman who asked what the reeds cost was sent to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}; the yard went around the clean dark line, the thaw, the space beneath the rack with its broken birth-slates, and the strip where a hand went in on Seed 15 and never came out: a look, a wide step, no number. One hundred and twenty-six days old, he read the arm as a record in muscle --- exact, worth nothing.

At the Cross a woman turned a cup a quarter on the pot board, set it back and went off with lead-glaze green at one corner of her mouth --- the third green at a mouth, no cause. Below the bridge the soft-cuffed clerk held his slate and the market sold over him; a girl with a creel took the out-of-line landing sideways.

Before first grey men came up the Clay Yard and spoke low in the room off the wheel-shed; Jorra Vail gave them no name, came through with slate dust ground into both forearms, told a pot \emph{You’ll do} and withheld its note from a High Kiln kiln-master. His bent finger went into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence. Berr Clay came up with his office cord folded, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, read \emph{one in twelve}, called the levy and denied it. That evening Tarn brought the ear-and-debt sentence to the word that would call the loan a second time and stopped there, no figure and no name. The boy filed it as a second interval, not a second payment.

At the Weir a reed-cutter turned his grey cord once on his thumb, tied one low with his teeth and put it back inside his coat: \emph{You can ask the cord} --- \emph{No more can the Court}. Orra Weir gave a date where a figure was asked; Mira Silt answered a thin run with \emph{Ask the river} and kept her thumb on the grey cord. Three doors down Alda Reed laid her birth-slates before the fold, crossed two fingers at the birth-flower, covered the sign with a dead woman’s date, said \emph{Warm and breathing}, and left six pages unread.

Sella set the boy on his bed, put the fold right, left the thread frozen, told the fire it was the thaw and said \emph{The house will keep it}. The river’s note came through the gap, the fire missed its fifth breath, the boards kept a knot: three counts, none become one. One hundred and twenty-eight days old, he was told by nobody; his hand went up an inch toward the water and came down, the count unspent.
\end{CRchronicle}
